Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimator

Source: R/trop.R
trop.Rd

trop() calculates the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) with the TROP estimator of Athey, Imbens, Qu, and Viviano (2026). A cell is one unit in one period. For each treated cell, a model calculates the outcome without the treatment. The model has two-way fixed effects and a low-rank term with a nuclear-norm penalty, and it uses only untreated cells. Unit weights decrease with the distance between the outcome history of a unit and the treated unit. Time weights decrease with the distance in periods.

Usage

trop(
  data,
  outcome,
  treatment,
  unit,
  time,
  method = c("local", "global"),
  lambda = NULL,
  grid = trop_grid(),
  cv_cells = NULL,
  n_placebo = 200L,
  placebo_size = 1L,
  max_cycles = 10L,
  se = c("bootstrap", "none"),
  n_boot = 200L,
  resample = c("stratified", "controls"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  ci = c("normal", "percentile"),
  control = trop_control(),
  seed = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  covariate_method = c("joint", "residualize"),
  target = NULL,
  strata = NULL,
  boot_rows = NULL,
  demean = FALSE,
  event_time = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame in long format with one row for each unit and period.

outcome, treatment, unit, time

Column names as strings. The treatment must be 0 or 1. Outcomes can be NA. The fits do not use these cells.

method

Use "local" or "global". Refer to the section Methods.

lambda

The tuning parameters as a named numeric vector or a named list with the names time, unit, and nn. If lambda is NULL, cross-validation selects the tuning parameters from grid.

grid

The tuning grids from trop_grid(), or "auto". With "auto", the function scales the default grid to the data. Refer to the section Tuning grid.

cv_cells

For the local method, the number of untreated cells in a random sample for the leave-one-out criterion. If cv_cells is NULL, the criterion uses all untreated cells, as in Eq. 5 of the paper.

n_placebo, placebo_size

For the global method, the number of placebo sets and the number of untreated units in each set. The defaults are the values of the Python package from the authors: 200 sets of 1 unit.

max_cycles

The maximum number of cycles of the coordinate search.

se

Use "bootstrap" for bootstrap standard errors or "none" for no standard errors.

n_boot

The number of bootstrap draws.

resample

Use "stratified" or "controls". Refer to the section Inference.

conf_level

The confidence level of the interval.

ci

Use "normal" or "percentile". The normal interval is the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times the bootstrap standard error. The percentile interval uses quantiles of the bootstrap draws. Refer to the section Inference.

control

The solver options from trop_control().

seed

An optional integer seed for the sampled cells, the placebo sets, and the bootstrap. The function does not change the state of the random number generator in the R session.

covariates

Optional names of numeric covariate columns. Refer to the section Covariates.

covariate_method

Use "joint" or "residualize". Refer to the section Covariates.

target

An optional name of a column with TRUE and FALSE (or 1 and 0) for each row of data. A treated cell with TRUE is in the estimate. Refer to the section Target cells. trop_matrix() takes a logical or 0/1 matrix with the dimensions of W.

strata

An optional name of a column with the stratum of each unit. The value must be the same for all rows of a unit. trop_matrix() takes a vector with one value for each unit. Refer to the section Inference.

boot_rows

An optional matrix of bootstrap draws from trop_boot_rows(). If you use it, n_boot and resample do not apply, and you cannot use strata.

demean

Logical. If TRUE, the function subtracts the mean of the untreated outcomes of each unit before it fits the model. Refer to the section Tuning grid.

event_time

An optional name of a numeric column with the event time of each row. Each treated row with an outcome must have a value. Refer to the section Event times. trop_matrix() takes a numeric matrix with the dimensions of W.

Value

An object of class trop. It is a list with these elements and with other elements:

  • estimate: the ATT.

  • std.error, conf.low, and conf.high: the bootstrap standard error and the confidence interval.

  • tau: a matrix with the effect for each treated cell.

  • lambda: the tuning parameters.

  • cv: the results of the cross-validation, or NULL for fixed tuning parameters. The element cv$boundary names the tuning values that are at the edge of the grid. Refer to the section Cross-validation scores.

  • boot: the bootstrap draws in draws, the kind of draws in resample, and the draw rows in rows. The element n_failed is the number of draws without an estimate. The element diagnostics has the counts of each draw.

  • n_excluded_cells: the number of treated cells that are not in the target.

  • covariates: NULL without covariates. Otherwise, a list with the coefficients coef, the method, and the names of the covariates that the function used and dropped.

  • panel: the matrices of the fit. trop_effects() uses them. They make the object larger.

  • package: the version of fasttrop, and its commit if it is known.

  • timing: the time in the C code and the total time, in seconds.

Methods

  • The local method (method = "local") is the estimator of Eq. 12 and Algorithm 2 of the paper. Each treated cell has its own unit weights, time weights, and fit. The leave-one-out criterion of Eq. 4 and Eq. 5 selects the tuning parameters. The coordinate search follows footnote 2 of the paper. You can use this method for block, staggered, and general designs.

  • The global method (method = "global") is the estimator of the Python package from the authors. It calculates one fit for a block design. The time weights decrease with the distance from the center of the treated block. The unit weights decrease with the distance from the average treated unit before the treatment. Placebo cross-validation on untreated units selects the tuning parameters. The coordinate search starts at the means of the grids.

Designs

In a block design, all treated units start the treatment in the same period and stay treated to the end of the panel. In a staggered design, the start periods are different, but the treatment does not stop. In a general design, the treatment stops for one or more units.

TWFE imputation

With lambda = c(time = 0, unit = 0, nn = Inf), both methods give TWFE imputation. This method fits unit effects and period effects to the untreated cells only. Then it subtracts the fitted value from the outcome of each treated cell.

A conventional TWFE regression is different. It uses all cells, and it has one coefficient for the treatment. In a block design with no NA outcomes, the two results are the same. In a staggered design, the results can be different if the effects are different between treated cells. The regression can give negative weights to some treated cells.

Inference

The unit bootstrap of Algorithm 3 of the paper gives the standard error. The bootstrap keeps the tuning parameters fixed. With resample = "stratified", the bootstrap draws treated and untreated units separately. With resample = "controls", the treated units do not change. The standard error is the standard deviation of the draws.

With strata, the bootstrap draws the units of each stratum separately. Each draw keeps the number of treated units and of untreated units in each stratum. Use this when the units are in groups, for example a rollout in waves.

With boot_rows, you give the draws. Use trop_boot_rows() to make them. If you give the same draws to two or more fits, the fits have a joint bootstrap distribution. Then trop_stepdown() can adjust the p-values of the fits. The draws and the panel are in the result, so trop_effects() can also calculate the effects of groups of cells.

The default interval is the normal interval with this standard error, as in the bootstrap variance of the paper. With ci = "percentile", the interval comes from quantiles of the draws, as in the Python package from the authors. A percentile interval is less accurate with a small number of draws. The paper also says that the bootstrap is correct only with many treated units. Thus, the function gives a warning message for a bootstrap with fewer than 5 treated units.

Target cells

By default, the estimate is the mean of the effects of all treated cells. With target, the estimate uses only some of the treated cells. For example, use target for the first 3 periods after the start of the treatment. The function does not use the outcome of a treated cell outside of the target, because the treatment can change it. The outcome is not in the fit of any other cell, and the cell is not in the estimate.

The result has the same value as a fit with NA in the outcome of these cells. The element n_excluded_cells of the result has the number of these cells.

The target is only for the local method, because the global method fits all treated cells together. Use trop_effects() to calculate the effects of many groups of cells in one fit.

Tuning grid

The default grid of trop_grid() fits an outcome with a standard deviation of about 1. If the outcome has other units, a better value can be outside of the grid. Then cross-validation chooses a value at the edge of the grid. The function gives a warning message when this happens for a finite value of time, unit, or nn. The result has the edge values in cv$boundary.

With grid = "auto", the function scales the default grid to the data with trop_grid_scaled(). With demean = TRUE, the function subtracts the mean of the untreated outcomes of each unit before it calculates the distances between units. The unit effect absorbs a constant of a unit. Thus, with unit = 0 the effects do not change. With a larger unit weight, the weights of the units are different. They compare the shape of the outcome histories and not the level.

Event times

trop_effects() and trop_cells() can make groups by event time and by cohort. By default, they find the start of each treatment run from W. The event time 0 is the first treated period of the run.

With event_time, you give the event time of each treated cell. Then the groups use these values, and the cohort of a cell is the period with the event time 0. Use the column event_time of trop_rollout().

The event time counts the periods of the panel. In a run of treated periods, it must increase by 1 from one period to the next. Thus, all cells of a run have the same cohort. A new run after an untreated period can have a different start. The function stops with an error if the event times do not agree with the runs of W.

The periods of the panel are the values of time in data. If no unit has a row for a period, the panel does not have this period. Then make the event times from the same data, or add a row with an NA outcome for this period.

Use event_time when the panel has no row for the start of a run. Also use it when the anticipation periods start before the first period of the panel. With event_time, do not give anticipation to trop_effects() and trop_cells(). The event times already count the anticipation periods.

A cell without a row has no outcome. In trop(), such a cell gets the treatment of its unit in the rows before and after it. Thus, a period without a row does not stop a treatment run. With event_time, the treated rows after the cell can show that their run starts after the cell. Then the cell gets W = 0, and a new run starts after it.

If the data have no rows just before the first treated row of a run, the start of the run is not certain. Then the function gives a warning message, unless you give event_time.

Cross-validation scores

The element cv$trace has one row for each tuning value that the search examined. The column score is the criterion. The column n_valid counts the cells in the score. For the local method, these are the held-out untreated cells with a prediction. For the global method, these are the placebo cells with an effect. The element cv$n_cells is the number of all such cells.

A score that uses fewer cells is not comparable. Thus, the search first prefers the tuning values with the largest n_valid. With the same n_valid, the smaller score is better. The function gives a warning if the chosen values do not use all cells. If no tuning value has a usable score, the function stops with an error.

Limits of the triple robustness result

Theorem 5.1 of the paper gives a bound for the bias. The bound is the product of three terms: the unit imbalance, the time imbalance, and the bias of the regression adjustment. The proof uses fixed weights, and it is only for a block design. For a staggered or general design, the function calculates the estimator, but the bound has no proof. Thus, the function gives a warning message for these designs.

Covariates

Section 6.2 of the paper adds a covariate term to the model of Eq. 13. The model has the fixed effects, the low-rank term, and a linear term \(X_{it}'\phi\). Use covariates to give the names of numeric columns. A row with an outcome must have finite values for all covariates. For a factor, make indicator columns with stats::model.matrix().

The paper gives the model, but it does not give one procedure to calculate \(\phi\). The function has two procedures:

  • With covariate_method = "joint", each weighted fit calculates \(\phi\) together with the fixed effects and the low-rank term. This is the minimization of Eq. 13. The local method calculates one \(\phi\) for each treated cell. The unit weights and the time weights use the outcomes, not the outcomes minus \(X'\phi\). The leave-one-out fits and the placebo fits also calculate \(\phi\).

  • With covariate_method = "residualize", the function first calculates \(\phi\) with an unweighted TWFE regression on all untreated cells with an outcome. Then it uses \(Y^* = Y - \tilde{X}\phi\) for the tuning, the weights, and the estimate. In \(\tilde{X}\), the function removes the unit effects and the period effects of the untreated cells from \(X\). The bootstrap calculates \(\phi\) again for each draw.

Section 6.2 of the paper tunes the estimator after it removes the covariates from the outcomes. The procedure "residualize" is one interpretation of that text. Usually, it does not give the minimum of Eq. 13. Its first step uses all untreated outcomes. Thus, the cells that the cross-validation holds out have an effect on \(\phi\).

The global method with covariates is an extension of fasttrop. The Python package from the authors does not have covariates.

The fixed effects absorb a term \(a_i + b_t\) in a covariate. Thus, the results do not change when you add a unit constant or a period constant to a covariate.

The function does not use a covariate that the unit effects, the period effects, or other covariates explain completely on the untreated cells. For example, a covariate that does not change in time has no effect on the estimate. The function gives a warning message for such a covariate. In a weighted fit with few untreated cells, a covariate can also have no variation. Then, that fit sets its coefficient to 0.

The element covariates$coef of the result contains \(\phi\) in the units of the covariates. For the local method with "joint", it is the mean of the values for the treated cells. This value is only a summary.

The appendix of the paper gives a bias bound with covariates. This bound adds a term: the imbalance of the covariates times the error in \(\phi\). Thus, the weights can decrease the bias, but they do not remove the bias from a wrong \(\phi\). A covariate that the treatment changes can also make a bias. Use only covariates that the treatment does not change.

References

Athey, S., Imbens, G. W., Qu, Z., and Viviano, D. (2026). Triply Robust Panel Estimators. Journal of Applied Econometrics. doi:10.1002/jae.70061 .

Examples

sim <- trop_simulate(n_units = 20, n_periods = 12, n_treated = 5,
                     n_post = 3, effect = 1, seed = 1)
fit <- trop(sim, "y", "d", "unit", "time",
            lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5),
            n_boot = 50, seed = 1, control = trop_control(threads = 1))
fit
#> Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimate
#>   Method: local | Design: block | Units: 20 | Periods: 12 | Treated cells: 15
#>   ATT: 1.119  (SE 0.202, 95% CI 0.7228 to 1.515)
#>   lambda: time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5
